It can also reduce driver attention, and conventional systems generally do not control downhill speed with the brakes. Is cruise control good for your car engine? Normal cruise-control use is generally not harmful to the engine. It may reduce abrupt acceleration and deceleration, but fuel and wear benefits vary with traffic, terrain, speed, and driving style. In many manual cars, pressing the clutch also disengages it, but button behavior varies by vehicle. How does cruise control work in a manual car? Manual-car cruise control controls throttle input to maintain the selected speed. Pressing the clutch during a gear change commonly cancels or temporarily interrupts the system, depending on the vehicle. What is the difference between cruise control and a speed limiter? Cruise control automatically maintains a target speed. A speed limiter sets a maximum speed but does not normally accelerate the car to maintain that speed.

What Is Cruise Control? The purpose of a cruise control system is to accurately maintain a speed set by the driver without any outside intervention by controlling the throttle-accelerator pedal linkage. The earliest forms of automatic speed regulation were actually in use even before the creation of automobiles. The inventor and mechanical engineer James Watt fitted his steam engines with a centrifugal (flyball) governor in 1788, which automatically adjusted the throttle to hold a constant speed as the engine load changed. Cruise control as we know it today, however, traces back to a blind American inventor named Ralph Teetor. He patented his "Speedostat" in 1950, and the technology reached the road in 1958 on select Chrysler models. Cadillac soon adopted it and rebranded it "Cruise Control," the name that stuck. passages.text: How does cruise control work on a car? Car cruise control maintains a driver-selected speed by comparing actual vehicle speed with a stored target, then adjusting the throttle through a cable, actuator, vacuum system, or electronic throttle. It adds power when speed drops, such as uphill, and reduces throttle when speed rises. Conventional cruise control generally does not brake, and the driver must continue steering, monitoring traffic, and remaining ready to cancel. What does cruise control do? Car cruise control maintains a selected speed without requiring continuous accelerator pressure. The system controls throttle input, but it does not steer the vehicle or replace the driver. Conventional cruise control is most useful on roads with steady traffic and gentle curves. The driver remains responsible for speed, lane position, traffic monitoring, and braking. How does cruise control maintain speed? Car cruise control uses a feedback loop to compare the vehicle's actual speed with the stored target. A controller then changes throttle input to correct the difference. The cruise control systems of some vehicles incorporate a "speed limiter" function, which will not allow the vehicle to accelerate beyond a preset maximum; this can usually be overridden by fully depressing the accelerator pedal. Most systems will prevent the vehicle from increasing engine speed to accelerate beyond the chosen speed. However, they will not apply the brakes in the event of over-speeding downhill, nor stop the car from going faster than the selected speed even with the engine just idling. Cruise control is less flexible on vehicles with a manual transmission because depressing the clutch pedal and shifting gears usually disengages the cruise control. The "resume" feature has to be used each time after selecting the new gear and releasing the clutch. Therefore, cruise control is most beneficial at motorway/highway speeds when top gear is used virtually all the time. The speed limiter function, however, does not have this problem. passages.text: Cruise control Cruise control (also known as speed control, cruise command, autocruise, or tempomat) is a system that automatically controls the speed of an automobile. The system is a servomechanism that takes over the car's throttle to maintain a steady speed set by the driver. History [edit] Speed control existed in early automobiles such as the Wilson-Pilcher in the early 1900s. They had a lever on the steering column that could be used to set the speed to be maintained by the engine.[1] In 1908, the Peerless included a governor to keep the speed of the engine through an extra throttle lever on the steering wheel.[2] Peerless successfully used a flyball governor.[3] They advertised their system as being able to "maintain speed whether uphill or down." A governor was used by James Watt and Matthew Boulton in 1788 to control steam engines, but the use of governors dates at least back to the 17th century. On an engine, the governor uses centrifugal force to adjust the throttle position to adapt the engine's speed to different loads (e.g., when going up a hill). When should you not use cruise control? Car cruise control should generally not be used on slippery roads, in poor weather, in heavy traffic, or when conditions change quickly. The driver should follow the owner's manual and posted speed limits. Avoid conventional cruise control in these situations: - Ice, snow, standing water, wet or slippery pavement - Fog or other conditions that reduce visibility - Rough, loose, winding, or sharply curving roads - Steep grades, especially when downhill speed may increase - Stop-and-go traffic or traffic requiring frequent reactions Adaptive cruise control still requires close supervision and may have vehicle-specific limits involving curves, stopped objects, lane changes, and automatic braking. Cancel the system and take direct control whenever traffic or road conditions become uncertain. Does cruise control save fuel or harm the car? Normal cruise-control operation is generally not harmful to the engine, transmission, or other vehicle systems.
